666 points by aarushyadav 14 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 331 comments
Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) (https://subvocal.company/). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech.
Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI
(Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.)
Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV...
We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology.
We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work:
- Signal changes due to sweat
- Electrical interference
- Placement variability
- Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!!
So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text.
Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc...
Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C...
This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas.
That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data.
So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration).
We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well.
Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases.
For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at https://subvocal.co/preorder!

title: knlb.dev | Resisting Cognitive Surrender
content:
Working Notes: a commonplace notebook for recording & exploring ideas.
Home. Site Map. Subscribe. More at expLog. — Kunal
Resisting Cognitive Surrender
sitemap / essays
Details
Contents
Cognitive surrender is seductive
Why not surrender?
Solutions
There are still tradeoffs
Choose your vibe limit & triage
Watch out for automation bias
Force yourself into the loop
Force comprehensibility
When you do decide to delegate
Good design is a force multiplier
Additional reading
Related
This particular note is around exploring cognitive surrender: uncritically accepting whatever agents output without actually thinking, exploring or considering alternatives. Working this way is extremely fast, not particularly taxing, and unsurprisingly seductive.
And yet I find myself repeatedly questioning if this is actually a good way to apply agents: often enough I find myself making suboptimal decisions, accruing technical debt and reducing my familiarity with the system I’m working on instead of improving it.
As we collectively rethink how we work I’ve been finding it useful to read and share other people’s workflows, and consciously write about and examine my own. This particular post focuses on finding the right balance of trust while working with agents.
Cognitive surrender is seductive
One of the virtues of being a great programmer is to be lazy. After more than a decade of training myself to look for the shortest and simplest path it’s rather attractive to be able to simply hand over the problem. If I can spin up a software factory, why wouldn’t I?
There’s also a lot of peer pressure (or game theory) at work: if any of my colleagues have seemingly surrendered, then I’m only going to look worse if I spend too much time trying to do silly things like understanding what I’m working on. And, of course, while everyone else is a slop-cannon generating code faster than they can read it I can build a meticulously designed software factory manufacturing perfect designs. The sheer volume of work also appears remarkably productive – we’ve all talked about just how many more PRs we ship every day.
This tends to get compounded by the agents’ expressed confidence & conviction. Perhaps an inadvertent consequence of RLHF, but models tend to be astonishingly confident in what they recommend (and perhaps even more blasé while admitting they made a mistake). This makes it too easy to take their answers at face value, with whatever social programming I seem to have evolved with.
OSS projects – particularly those facing time pressure – seem to accrue tremendous complexity quickly, to the point that it feels like the only way to interact with a project in any sane time frame is by heavily relying on agents to navigate and modify and test the code. This is also a self-reinforcing feedback loop: broken windows multiply rapidly with agents on the loose. [1]
Technical debt and incidental complexity have a fairly attenuated feedback loop: complexity introduced by slop doesn’t bite immediately; it’s far more subtle and compounds over time when I’m not paying attention.
Beyond all of that, I have to mention the hype cycle. We all should be skipping Netflix to watch talks by Anthropic engineers on making loops (or the agentic workflow du jour). [2]
Why not surrender?
It’s not entirely obvious that it’s a bad idea to surrender: if it’s easier and better, then why not take that path? So far, my personal answer is that I need to take the easier path consciously and intentionally, with enough effort to mitigate downsides.
Part of what makes me deeply uncomfortable is suffering from a form of Gell-Mann amnesia while working with agents. When I have expertise and the overall design direction I can generally simplify the output significantly, controlling for complexity. When I don’t they seem to be the smartest engineers in existence – far beyond the more squishy, organic variety – and all I can do is follow in awe. And then the agent gets stuck creating a directory and I have to reset all my assumptions.
For the current state of the art (October 2026) I generally find maximal use of agents leads to a significant explosion in complexity: something that mostly works, with extremely surprising edge cases and bugs. These are generally the projects with hundreds of thousands of lines of code shipped rapidly, breaking the scale supported by most software development tools, so you also need to revisit those – and this compounds rapidly.
I have a strong aversion to incidental complexity, and generally refuse to build, maintain or extend it: it’s fine for a proof-of-concept, but it must end there. For systems that need to keep working, steering the design aggressively towards simplicity and modularity is what lets me build something I can actually operate (with and without agents).
As models continue to improve rapidly, I expect the previous argument to go away as the models learn and can express a broader sense of engineering taste, good design and quality. The other reason – which I unfortunately expect to persist – is that my personal understanding and mechanical sympathy for systems I maintain erode extremely rapidly, or never get a chance to develop.
In the early days when I would build things by hand I’d be able to quickly diagnose any bug or misbehavior based on my familiarity with building and maintaining the code: the more I rely on agents, the more my only option is to spin up one more session and hope; and the automated fix then further reduces my understanding in a self-reinforcing loop. Without context, I no longer have much meaningful judgement and can’t engage – or handle it in context.
The Ironies of Automation (1983) is referred to often in articles similar to this one. I’d recommend directly reading the paper if you haven’t: it’s fully relevant to the decisions we have to make today. The paper warns that it becomes even harder to deal with tasks an agent fails at because we never manage to get any practice with the easier tasks; nor do we get a chance to internalize what a system feels like under standard operating circumstances.
At the end of the day, I’m responsible and accountable for what I build, not the agents. Surrendering agency and not thinking basically makes me accountable without any meaningful ownership. There’s also the small matter of pride in the quality of my work.[3]
Solutions
The sombre opening shouldn’t lead you to believe that I’m not excited about the sheer potential unlocked by AI, and the opportunities to build things that I would never have been able to without it. It’s more about resetting expectations, explicitly working through the tradeoffs involved and choosing which ones are acceptable. And finding ways to maintain the quality and craftsmanship I care about.
There are still tradeoffs
The first step for me has been to internalize that I can’t truly have my cake and eat it: I can go terribly, inhumanly fast at building things but I need to accept that there’s no way to retain the mechanical sympathy, depth and confidence I used to have without putting in the effort. Time that used to be only counted as building a system also involved comprehension; agents can drive the time to build to zero but the next bottleneck – comprehension – hasn’t moved much so far.
The hype cycle occasionally can make it hard to communicate this explicitly: a lot of the communication around agentic loops tends to assume that there are no downsides whatsoever.
Choose your vibe limit & triage
Several months ago I defined my vibe limit as the complexity of the change I can make with sufficient confidence using agents. I like the risk/complexity curve enough to post it again:
The next step is figuring out where I land: there are several projects where good enough is fine, or the problem is sufficiently sandboxed that I’m happy to live with whatever the agents generated. On the other hand, if the system is important, fragile, can’t be sanity checked easily or isn’t particularly well isolated I need to directly spend my time.
Aggressive prioritization, triage, and constantly recalibrating myself become really important in this ecosystem: I should explicitly choose where to surrender agency and where to spend my time (not unlike leading a team, except the pace is much faster). Constantly reviewing my predictions and the outcomes helps a lot in recalibrating, particularly with new model drops.
Watch out for automation bias
I also find myself needing to be much more mindful while working. A warning sign I watch out for these days is if I find myself repeatedly tapping “yes, continue” in a session. At that point either I should figure out what it would take to completely delegate the problem to Claude instead of trying to micro-manage the agent – or realize that I stopped thinking and I need to check the decisions being made.
Completely delegating the problem generally means building a better sandbox or feedback loop, or figuring out ways to be able to sanity check much more easily before shipping to production. Alternatively, if I need to engage much more deeply I’ll use some of the other tactics described below.
Force yourself into the loop
The premise of augmenting myself by working in the loop with powerful thinking machines was a large part of my decision to join my current company. This generally comes down to directions you can give the model to reduce the size of the steps it takes, or explicitly choosing to drive instead of passively observing.
For projects I deeply care about, choosing to drive instead of letting the model drive is one way to intervene in every single decision. It’s much slower to type things out, but it does force me to engage with every decision and gives me an opportunity to override it. In fact, for this post I’m using a Codex session to edit: help me tighten the post, point out the small typos, punctuation errors, or half-finished sentences that tend to embarrass me after I explicitly share a post publicly – but I make all changes by hand.
In the AGENTS.md for the notebook:
Never edit files directly, always wait for the author to request or confirm changes, or let him make the edits directly.
This is reminiscent of how I used to work with Stack Overflow: never copy-paste code; instead write it out explicitly while cross-checking with documentation. Either I’d learn and internalize something new or I’d realize the Stack Overflow answer was suboptimal or outdated.
Force comprehensibility
We don’t need to limit ourselves to existing interfaces anymore: with agents it’s also possible to have them build a tremendous amount of scaffolding to support comprehension and make changes in ways that are digestible.
Often enough for larger, complex stacks I have the agents build me a custom view for the Pull Request with 4 columns: the standard 2 for the diff, a 3rd column with running commentary from the agent on why it made a particular change and finally the 4th column as a place for me to add comments and directions.
Getting the agents to make stacks of changes with the explicit direction to “Make the change easy, then make the easy change” works really well. I used to spend a lot of time trying to make my diffs easily reviewable to respect the reviewers’ time – now I can ask the agents to do the same for me.
It’s also very valuable to dive into actual execution with a debugger (or have an agent manipulate the debugger on your behalf) till you get a deep sense of how things are flowing through the program, with the confidence that this is the real execution path.
Another example is to make harnesses explain what they’re doing: I’ve built several variations of command-line helpers that transparently fit into my shell sessions (x being the last public version). In my most recent iteration, I explicitly ask the model to explain any obscure flags and commands used so that I can learn as I go.
When you do decide to delegate
Sometimes, it does make sense to hand over the problem to an agent: it could be too big, not valuable enough, time could be too short, or you just want to get a first prototype out to explore a problem end-to-end.
This one is probably an essay by itself: adapting old-school best practices when you have infinitely fast stochastic intelligence on top. The idea here is to reduce the risk in making changes, flattening the vibe-limit curve and making it possible to make bigger changes safely.
Beyond giving the agent some means to verify itself against the goal you’re aiming for, I find it very useful to:
Observability: Invest heavily in observability, both black-box and white-box, and make sure to keep a direct handle on the metrics instead of solely relying on the agents’ view. As a habit I prefer to triangulate onto a behavior with multiple sources of metrics, and that becomes even more important with systems rapidly becoming opaque.
Non-functional requirements: Don’t forget to observe resource utilization and other non-functional requirements: these can be canaries for unexpected behavior.
Deterministic validation: Build mechanical straitjackets for the model: have held-out pieces of code or deterministic tools for validation and observations as a hold-out against the model misunderstanding or glitching.
Shadow Traffic: Make it possible and cheap to run a deployed candidate against shadow traffic with no side effects: keep it as similar to production as possible, and this can be the final gate to prevent surprises.
Style guides: Give the model a style guide based on your existing code and work. I’ve found Claude’s output far more to my taste after having the models generate a style guide based on all the code and blog posts I’ve written in the past.
Fast deploys: An often maligned motto at Facebook used to be Move Fast & Break Things: that, too, is an intentional tradeoff to make. If you can’t be sure of quality, make it very easy to deploy code as well – so changes can be shipped and reverted extremely rapidly.
Rethink what’s possible: It’s surprisingly easy to write and rewrite systems from scratch rapidly as you learn. Build to throw, evaluate, and repeat to get something knocked into great shape – I’ve built projects in multiple iterations, giving the agent the previous iteration and its limitations as initial context and constantly finding myself able to deeply increase the quality. This doesn’t work as well when you’re punishing your code reviewers though, so make sure to align with your team, or simply don’t get the first several iterations reviewed.
Good design is a force multiplier
In Notes on the Synthesis of Form Christopher Alexander has a wonderful example demonstrating the value of decomposition – or building a lightly coupled, cohesive system to be able to succeed quickly.
No complex adaptive system will succeed in adapting in a reasonable amount of time unless the adaptation can proceed subsystem by subsystem, each subsystem relatively independent of the others.
Whether agents or humans are doing the work, a g

Galactus the Devourer
On efficient algorithms, the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and losing the plot.
BEN RECHT
OCT 30, 2026
121
17
20
Share
Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post is about the history of failing to rigorously define efficiency in computer science. Like my previous post on Fourier transforms, it’s more technical than usual, but I tried to make it as accessible as possible.
I’ve always been fascinated by this pernicious pattern in the practice of applied mathematics, which I wrote about here a few weeks ago:
Applied mathematicians often need to build a giant scaffolding of mathematical modeling to solve a problem. This scaffolding creates new mathematical puzzles that aren’t directly connected to the original problem of interest, but that entice problem solvers. You’ll then see dozens of follow-up papers solving the puzzles but forgetting the problem we cared about in the first place.
There is probably no better example of such forgetting than the field of complexity theory.
In 1965, Jack Edmonds came up with a clever way to find a maximum matching in a graph. He wanted to argue that his algorithm could be computed “efficiently,” as the procedure was a bit complicated and required a computer to run. But he found he didn’t have the language to describe what it would mean for an algorithm to be efficient. In Section 2 of his paper, named “Digression,” he wrote,
According to the dictionary, “efficient” means “adequate in operation or performance.” This is roughly the meaning I want—in the sense that it is conceivable for maximum matching to have no efficient algorithm. Perhaps a better word is “good.”
I am claiming, as a mathematical result, the existence of a good algorithm.
Edmonds noted that he could enumerate every possible solution to the matching problem and find the largest one. This would be a correct algorithm. However, the number of total matchings is exponentially large in the size of the graph. Blindly writing all possible matchings down and picking the one that achieved the maximum was a “not good” algorithm. You might call it a “bad” algorithm. His new procedure was vastly more efficient.
So Edmonds spent two pages constructing a definition of good. He demanded that everyone agree on a reasonable definition for a problem size. For his matching problem, he said the size was the number of vertices plus the number of edges in the graph. A good algorithm would then have a running time upper-bounded by some well-defined function of that size, no matter how large the instance. He demanded that the running-time bound hold for every conceivable size, because he feared someone might rig the problem by planting a few small instances that were unnaturally hard.
Edmonds wasn’t completely satisfied with this definition. Indeed, he wrote:
It would be unfortunate for any rigid criterion to inhibit the practical development of algorithms which are either not known or known not to conform nicely to the criterion. Many of the best algorithmic ideas known today would suffer by such theoretical pedantry. In fact, an outstanding open question is, essentially: “how good” is a particular algorithm for linear programming, the simplex method? And, on the other hand, many important algorithmic ideas in electrical switching theory are obviously not “good” in our sense.1
With this caveat noted, he concluded his digression by announcing the complexity of his new blossom algorithm: “An upper bound on the order of difficulty of the matching algorithm is n4, where n is the number of vertices in the graph.”
Edmonds did not make any further arguments for what he meant by good. He asserted that exponential time is bad. For most algorithm designers, linear time, proportional to the input length, was naturally excellent. Moreover, our grade-school multiplication algorithm took quadratic time (multiply two three-digit numbers out by hand like you were taught in school and count the number of digits you write down when you calculate it), and that seemed pretty good. Edmonds had a matching algorithm that required a quartic number of operations. To later formalists like Richard Karp, it seemed like a “polynomial” number of operations was a reasonable definition for goodness. Polynomial time is good. Exponential time is bad. This created the field of complexity theory, with the goal of proving that all sorts of algorithms run in polynomial time and characterizing the problems for which no polynomial-time algorithm existed.
But polynomial time probably haunted Edmonds. It is not a “good” algorithm if your procedure scales like n1000, even if this is technically a polynomial. More absurdly,
is a polynomial bigger than the exponential function 2n for any n we could ever encounter. Polynomial was always an imperfect definition of good, but we ran with it. Thousands of papers later, we just have a zoo of confusing complexity results unmoored from the realities of computation.
Indeed, asymptotic thinking about how polynomials differ from exponentials enables the bad habit of designing “galactic algorithms,” conceptual procedures with running times so large they could never be implemented in our universe. I mentioned these in my earlier post about OpenAI’s Faster Fourier Transform.
This brings me back to our beneficent friends at OpenAI. This week they declared their latest breakthrough in theoretical computer science. They provided an algorithm for the satisfiability problem that ran in “subexponential time.” Satisfiability is one of the most well-known “NP complete problems, and I don’t want to go into the details of P vs NP today, but suffice it to say that you would win a Clay Millennium Prize if you could find a polynomial-time algorithm for satisfiability.2
Now, subexponential time does not mean polynomial time. It merely means that the running time can be bounded as
Where n is the problem size, and f is a “sublinear” function, meaning the limit of f(n)/n goes to zero as n goes to infinity.
Indeed, in the case of OpenAI’s new algorithm for the satisfiability problem, the bound was
For some unspecified constant numbers d and C. Ugly as this expression is, this was touted on Twitter as the biggest moment in theoretical computer science in 50 years. It was covered all over the tech press this week. OpenAI clearly wanted us to think it was a big fucking deal. And many theoretical computer scientists took to social media to agree.
Since it was such a big deal, I wanted to see if I could understand the algorithm a bit. Of course, as I’ve told all of you, we’re not supposed to read these papers. We’re supposed to ask ChatGPT what they say. And ChatGPT told me there was a catch.
The derived algorithm runs exhaustive search—the algorithm Edmonds declared bad in 1965—if the number of variables is less than 10^10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000.
This is a completely unfathomable number.3 There are something like 10^80 atoms in the universe. That’s 10^9,999,999,999,999,999,999,999,920 times smaller. Up until this barely finite threshold, the magic new algorithm calls an exponential-time subroutine. For any problem that we could ever consider, the procedure is exponential time. The “result” is that only in some bizarre, unknowable neighborhood of infinity, satisfiability problems are solved in subexponential time.
The claimed subexponential algorithm for satisfiability is definitive evidence that our definition of efficient was even worse than we thought it was 50 years ago. The answer tells us nothing about efficiency or goodness. Sometimes you need to answer your question to realize you wanted something else.
I’m not a betting man, but I have a prediction. It’s going to turn out that P=NP in some galactic sense, and all we’ll learn is that we spent fifty years answering the wrong question.
Subscribe
1
It’s funny that Edmonds references the simplex algorithm in his musings here. The simplex algorithm is the most important algorithm ever invented, and we now know that, technically speaking, its running time is exponential. Most of the time it’s fast, but you can construct weird cases where it takes an exponential number of steps. And yet, it is deployed all over the globe, determining optimal programs for exponentially diverse applications in optimization. Edmonds foresaw this sharp disconnect between theory and practice in 1965!
2
What’s particularly ironic is that we have incredibly efficient algorithms to solve industrial-scale satisfiability problems. Conventional computers can solve problems with millions of variables and millions of clauses. This guy at Intel solved a problem with a billion variables and 4 billion clauses in a day.
3
I confirmed this crazy number by plugging the paper into Claude. ChatGPT and Claude hate each other, so if they agree, it must be true.

title: Toit v2.0.0 — Toit blog
content:
← THE TOIT BLOG
Toit v2.0.0
Celebrating Toit v2.0.0 after more than four years of alpha development.
October 31, 2026 · Florian Loitsch
After more than four years of alpha development, 2,000+ commits, 500,000+ lines changed, and 200+ alpha releases, Toit v2.0.0 is finally here.
Toit began as closed-source software developed by Toitware. It later became an open-source project, and volunteers have continued improving it even after Toitware shut down in 2024.
Despite the "alpha" label, Toit has been stable for a long time. Two things kept us from calling it v2.0.0: we still had some breaking changes planned, and there was always another important feature we wanted to include.
Recently, we landed a refactoring that lets peripheral APIs accept pin numbers directly instead of requiring gpio.Pin objects. That was the last major breaking change on our list for v2.0.0.
As for waiting until all the important features are finished: we have accepted that this moment will never come. Even now, there are open PRs for a formatter, compiler resolution improvements, and support for more architectures, among other major features. Those will follow in future releases.
Here are a few highlights since Toit was open-sourced:
Broader hardware support, including the Arm-based EC618 and almost all ESP32 variants.
A unified toit command and improvements that make Toit a more capable desktop scripting language.
A rewritten package manager and a growing package ecosystem.
Mixins for sharing implementations across classes.
Firmware envelopes, allowing users to customize their firmware without rebuilding the SDK.
Compiler and runtime improvements.
Significantly better hardware testing.
Syntax highlighting for Toit on GitHub.
Enjoy!

title: If you love a website, back it up - The Future Is Now
content:
If you love a website, back it up
OCT 29TH, 2026 4:21 PM
This story starts with a little tragedy. See, I’ve got these old webpages I love to go back and look on every now and then. There’s websites that have been online unchanged for years and years, or decades, and there’s something a little cozy about checking in on them every now and then to see an old friend is still doing okay. Sometimes, of course, tragedy strikes.
There was this fansite called teapuppies.com for an old anime series and and toy line called Ochaken. It’s about these cute cartoon dog characters who have tea leaves for ears, each of them named after a different kind of tea.1 The site had been online since 2004 and had basically not changed since 2005, but it was nice just having it around. Except when I went to visit it a few weeks ago, and discovered that not only was the site gone but the domain is now being used to serve online gambling ads.
I work in web archiving, by the way. Which is to say that I should have known the site would go offline someday, and that I have the tools to have done something about it. I could have archived that site while it was still around, but I didn’t. This post is here to beg you to do what I didn’t think to, and to teach you how.
You see, when I talk to a lot of people about web archiving, they always seem to believe it’s something they couldn’t do. It’s something a big organization like the Internet Archive does, and if you want a webpage to be saved you just have to wait and hope it gets done. But that’s not true! What I really want everyone to know is that you have control over the world around you, you can take action to preserve things and make things better. And not just can, but should! Don’t just wait for someone else to act - get out there and and make it happen! Got a favourite site? Back it up! Got some information you don’t want to get lost? Back it up! Favourite post somewhere? All together now. Back! It! Up!
All of the tools I’ll be showing off in this post use standard web archiving formats like WARC2. You don’t have to worry about any of the technical details3, but I’m telling you that because it means there are a lot of really great tools to do whatever you want with them. Here, just as an example, is an entire archived website embedded right in this blog post:
You can even click through all the links, look at all of the images, the works. It’s an entire website right in a post! (And if you don’t trust me to keep this up, and you want the web archive to host somewhere else? You can download it for yourself right from there. Just click the kebab menu and choose “download archive”, and you can do whatever you like with it. In fact, please do!)
By the way, for disclosure: the tools I’m going to mention in this blog post are made by the company I work for, but that’s not because they’ll pay my salary (most of them are free!). I just happen to think these are the best tools there are for personal web archiving.
Option 1 - ArchiveWeb.page browser extension
By far the easiest personal web archiving tool is the ArchiveWeb.page browser extension for Chrome. This doesn’t take much in the way of setup or technical skills, and it works for anything: a single page, an entire website, a social media post or profile. So long as you can see it in a web browser, you can save it. All you really need to do is:
Install the browser extension.
Visit the first page you want to archive.
Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click “Start Archiving”.
If your page has any interactive elements, click on those to make sure all their data loads.
Visit any other pages you want captured in the same collection and let the extension grab them.
Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click “Stop Archiving”.
You’re done! You just archived a web page! Now that it’s all saved, you can preview it and see how it went by clicking the extension’s icon and then the home icon to open the extension dashboard. From there, you can click on your archiving session to preview the pages you archived, load them in browser, and see if they work. (I’ll go into more details on how you can look at web archives and share them with others later in this post.)
Option 2 - archiveweb.page app
If you don’t want to install a browser extension, or you don’t have Chrome installed, you can also grab the standalone archiveweb.page app. This is basically the same thing as the browser extension above, it just has its own web browser built in. It also opens straight to the menu that lets you browse your web archives, so it’s a handy way to look at your web archives locally. Pretty much everything else I described above applies.
Option 3 - Browsertrix
The above options are great for single pages or sites that are small enough for you to browse manually. But if you’ve got a webpage that’s big enough that it’s going to be annoying visiting all of the pages by hand, you probably want to look at a web crawler tool for web archiving. There are a bunch of options out there, but the easiest to use as an individual is probably Browsertrix. A web crawler is basically an automation tool built around a web browser; you provide instructions on what page to start from and what pages it should visit, and it will go ahead and click links to automatically find pages so that it can archive the page as completely as possible. The web archive I embedded above was done using Browsertrix on pretty close to its default settings: I just told it I wanted to do a site crawl for the entire domain https://teapuppies.mistys-internet.website, and it worked it out from there:
But, depending, on what you’re looking for, it has options which can be customized to narrow down what content it archives. For example, if you decided you only want pages for the episodes, you could tell it to only capture anything at the /episodes/ section of the website:
Or even just a single page and anything that page links to:
There are a lot more options than I can go into in a quick overview - it’s a comprehensive tool with a lot of options. But if you’re looking to archive a whole website, or a complete social media profile, I’d recommend giving it a try.
Unlike the other tools, which you mainly run on your own computer, Browsertrix is primarily a web app. It’s also the only paid tool in this post - there’s a seven day trial, but after that you do have to pay per use. Since it’s open source, though, technically inclined users can run their own copies on their computer or deploy a copy somewhere if they like.
Viewing your archived webpage
Once you’ve actually backed the site up, you can replay it to use it in your browser just like a live webpage. It’s kind of like having your own private version of the wayback machine. You can test it out yourself for your own private use using the interface built into the version of archiveweb.page you used, but if you want to share it with someone else you have a few options. If you want to share it with someone privately, you can send them the WARC/WACZ file and let them load it into the ArchiveWeb.page app or the ReplayWeb.page website. If you want to share it with the world, though, you can set up a website with your web archive on it.
This post is using the ReplayWeb.page embedded viewer, which is open source and can be embedded inside any other web page you want. You don’t have run any kind of app on your server to do this; as long as you have the ability to upload the archive and a little bit of JavaScript, you can easily add a copy of the replay interface into any web page or blog post.
Preserving the data once you have it
Since everything you backed up is bundled inside a single WACZ file, it’s really easy to keep safe - or share with someone else. Lots of copies keeps stuff safe, after all; if you think you have friends who’d like to hold on to a copy of whatever site you’ve backed it up, pass it along and share the duty of preserving it!
If any of this sounds interesting to you, I’d encourage you to at least give it a try. I’d love for the world to be filled with thousands upon thousands of little web archives, with people and community groups archiving and sharing the things that matter to them for themselves. If you’re finding any of this overwhelming, and you’re not sure where to get started, please reach out to me - I’m very happy to give you a hand.
The appeal to me is, I hope, obvious. ↩
Most of the tools I’m mentioning also use the WACZ format, which packages up WARC files along with extra metadata. ↩
For those who want a little extra technical detail, though: one of the things that makes WARC special is that it records complete information about requests and responses, including all headers. This gives WARC a much more complete view of the whole process of visiting a website, and makes it possible to archive even complicated sites with client-side JavaScript that make a ton of requests. ↩

Self-Employed? Solopreneur? NIST Has a Cybersecurity Guide Just for You
November 2, 2026
Share
A new NIST guide can help solo business owners — also called “solopreneurs” — grasp the basics of cybersecurity and craft a strategy that can help reduce their cybersecurity risk.
The guide is designed to help solopreneurs prioritize and implement a selection of actions from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework that would best help their businesses.
The publication is written in lay language and assumes no prior cybersecurity knowledge.
Credit: Asian Isolated/Shutterstock
If you work for yourself, as millions of Americans do, protecting your business from cyberattack is one of many responsibilities that falls entirely on your shoulders. Don’t feel daunted: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has just released a guide with your needs — and busy life — in mind.
Small Business Cybersecurity: Non-Employer Firms (NIST Cybersecurity White Paper 50) is a lay-language resource offering cybersecurity basics tailored expressly to the “solopreneur” — a term referring to anyone who is a business’s sole paid employee. More than 28 million small businesses in the U.S. fall into the solopreneur category, existing in every industry and forming a substantial part of the economy. The publication is written to introduce solopreneurs to the fundamentals of a small-business cybersecurity program and provide an actionable approach to implementing it.
“Because solopreneurs may not have cybersecurity expertise, we wanted to create a resource designed for them,” said NIST’s Daniel Eliot, one of the publication’s authors. “They can implement many of these actions on their own with limited technical knowledge or with minimal financial investment.”
The publication is an update to what was previously titled Small Business Information Security: The Fundamentals (NISTIR 7621). While that publication was aimed at small businesses of varying sizes and covered the broader topic of information security, the revision is narrower in scope and concentrates on protecting digital systems from malicious attack. The updated publication draws its guidelines from the well-known NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF 2.0), though the new publication is written with the novice in mind.
“This publication assumes the reader has no familiarity with cybersecurity or the NIST CSF,” Eliot said. “We want to educate people about what cybersecurity is and how it fits in with a successful business plan. We know solopreneurs are often very busy people, so any time we introduce a topic or throw out jargony terms, we try to provide context and definitions for the lay reader.”
The publication’s opening section, which includes the introduction and a chapter on the NIST CSF, is essentially a primer on cybersecurity and how it can support a solopreneur’s business.
“In addition to the general context, we highlight a set of actionable best practices that significantly reduce cybersecurity risks. These include regular data backups and maintaining updated software,” Eliot said. “They are a good set of first steps a small business might take.”
The central section offers specific actions from the CSF that can be implemented in a solo business. For each of these actions, the guide includes the rationale for performing it, how the business can get started, and options for what to do later as the business grows. Each action offers a brief citation that maps to the relevant section in the CSF and often references additional resources, so that interested readers can learn more.
For example, one recommended action is to change the default passwords that a manufacturer assigns to a device, as is common with Wi-Fi routers and other networked items. The rationale is that criminals can easily find these default passwords and use them to access the device. The business can get started by reviewing the security settings on all devices and creating unique, strong passwords for them. As the business grows, it can establish procedures for device onboarding and management to ensure it manages passwords securely.
Closing the document is a set of tools to help with implementing the central section’s actions, such as worksheets for inventorying at-risk assets or tracking all the actions the business has taken. Included here are three “use cases” — hypothetical solopreneurs including a lawyer, an artisan and a business consultant — that can help solopreneurs visualize and plan their own cybersecurity strategy.
“Working through these guidelines can help a solopreneur develop a strong foundation in cybersecurity,” Eliot said. “The publication is not comprehensive and won’t address all the needs of every solopreneur, because every reader will have different levels of cybersecurity knowledge and sophistication. But it does provide a good starting point for solo business owners that need one.”

title: [2608.25820] Open-Source 5G RAN Platforms: A Dual Perspective on Performance and Capabilities
content:
Computer Science > Networking and Internet Architecture
[Submitted on 26 Aug 2026]
Open-Source 5G RAN Platforms: A Dual Perspective on Performance and Capabilities
Maria Katarine Santana Barbosa, Iasmin Gomes, Vinícius Melo, Kelvin Lopes Dias
Open-source implementations of the fifth generation (5G) Radio Access Network (RAN), such as OpenAirInterface (OAI) and srsRAN, have become increasingly relevant for industry and academic research, rapid prototyping, and low-cost private 5G deployments. The state of the art presents different evaluation scenarios for both platforms; however, these are often limited to individual testbed evaluations, end-to-end studies, or partial comparisons between them. In particular, there is a lack of evaluations considering different Software-Defined Radios (SDRs), RAN configurations, user applications, and numbers of real UEs. To address this gap, this paper presents a comparative evaluation of OAI and srsRAN. The study includes a qualitative assessment of supported features and deployment flexibility, followed by a quantitative performance analysis covering radio resource control setup procedures, compliance with theoretical data rates, and real application workloads with diverse quality of service requirements. Specifically, we consider Video on Demand (VoD) for data rate evaluation, Live Streaming (LS) and Cloud Gaming (CG) as latency-sensitive applications. These workloads provide a comprehensive view of each platform capability.

title: nixos on 512mb ram — LowEndSpirit
content:
Shrinking NixOS Ram footprint and resource requirements to the bare minimum.
AnthonySmith
2500+ karma
AdministratorProviderOG
October 30
edited October 30
14 min read
Originally written by
AnthonySmith
·
Read the original forum post
A few people were surprised by how low you can go with NixOS, so i thought I would do a write up as I did not realise this was anything special, I kept notes when doing it but not for the intention of writing a blog article so i might miss small tweaks I did here and there.
I initially set aside half a day for this; it actually took closer to 3 days.
This guide is not very focused on saving disk space. If you want a disk space saving guide that has already been done by someone else here: https://nixcademy.com/posts/minimizing-nixos-images/ this has its own set of challenges and drawbacks so if you want to layer them together, be my guest I have decided not to implement the disk-minimising options into the TierHive NixOS template as I feel it is too likely to cause a default that end users are unlikely to expect.
Here we go:
NixOS 26.05 idling at around 96MB and rebuilding in 512MB
Stock deployment before any changes and with cloud-init, it runs on 1024MB RAM, JUST!, it sat at 288MB used with 89 kernel modules loaded, and a plain same-release rebuild needed 896MB (at 768 nix-build got OOM-killed at 505MB anon).
It now idles at 96MB used on a 512MB VPS with 54 modules, and a full channel update plus rebuild, including a kernel switch to 7.3 if you want to do that, It finishes at 512MB with a 371MB peak and no OOM. All numbers are from my own runs sometimes I recorded exact numbers others I left out the KB's and only recorded the MB's , measured a few minutes after the second boot with nobody logged in using my own build environment testing tools (I never log in to templates before use so they are clean)
Roughly in the order and things done on this template (even the harmless fails):
sysctl.vm.mem_profiling=never on the cmdline. The NixOS kernel ships with allocation profiling enabled by default and the tracking tables cost about 6MB (3.9MB vmalloc, 1.9MB slab). the bare mem_profiling=never which is left in isn't a valid parameter; the kernel juts hands it to userspace and nothing changes, it needs the sysctl. prefix.
kfence.sample_interval=0 gets back the 2MB KFENCE pool.
damon_stat.enabled=N and audit=0 get rid of the kdamond and kauditd threads.
initcall_blacklist=ksm_init,tpm_init,init_tis drops ksmd (1.4MB) and the TPM bits (0.3MB plus a kthread). No TPM in these guests and KSM inside a guest is pointless. (For TierHive anyway)
psi=0 ras=cec_disable nowatchdog nmi_watchdog=0 cryptomgr.notests 8250.nr_uarts=1 are all small, mostly fewer kthreads and less noise. On a 2GB test VM the whole cmd line set took non-cache memory from 128.0 to 121MB and kthreads from 64 to 59.
transparent_hugepage=never was one of the biggest single wins. With THP on madvise the kernel bumps vm.min_free_kbytes to 41108 (3710 without THP at 896MB), which is reserved memory you never get to use. Turning it off freed 52MB at 2GB and gave 103MB more available at 896MB, obviously in high end or production there are reasons not to do this, but day to day use, you probably wont notice any difference.
Blacklisted the hardware a KVM guest never has or doesn't need: floppy, intel_agp, i2c_piix4, psmouse, mousedev, joydev, serio_raw, evdev, button (using tiny_power_button already handles ACPI shutdown), the rapl/cstate/uncore lot, kvm, cfg80211 (networkd was pulling it in for nl80211), ata_generic/pata_acpi, qemu_fw_cfg, dmi_sysfs, vga16fb.
Blacklisted virtio_console as well, nothing uses the agent channel and it was holding an 8MB kmalloc-4k slab.
vsock, vmci and virtiofs get install <mod> /bin/false rather than a blacklist. They get requested at switch-root with no device present, and with a plain blacklist vmw_vmci just loaded instead.
Blacklisted virtio_gpu and let the VNC console run on plain vgacon through virtio-vga. That one was really for a 6.18.59 fix/workaround, it does not follow to 7.3 but thats optional I guess.
Initrd cut down to virtio_pci virtio_blk ext4 with includeDefaultModules = false, without importing the qemu-guest profile.
Trimmed the kernel module tree with a small derivation that replaces system.modulesTree. It drops sound, GPU, wifi, USB, physical NIC, SCSI/ATA HBA drivers and so on, always keeping the deps of anything it keeps. 162MB down to 45MB on disk, and udev has nothing silly left to autoload. It runs inside nixos-rebuild so kernel updates get the same treatment for free.
Disabled systemd-resolved, 8.3MB PSS and it was listening for LLMNR/mDNS on 0.0.0.0:5355. cloud-init writes a plain resolv.conf instead.
Swapped systemd-timesyncd (4.6MB) for a oneshot busybox ntpd -n -q on a timer, at boot and hourly, so nothing stays resident (won't work everywhere but on most KVM hosts it should be fine)
services.openssh.startWhenNeeded = true so sshd is socket activated and the 3.9MB listener only exists while someone is connected. (Perfect for NAT but if you are sitting with port 22 listening for connections on a public IP you might want to skip this)
Disabled systemd-oomd (1.8MB).
A tiny oneshot drops LLDP=no into the cloud-init generated .network files, which stops the networkd LLDP socket and af_packet loading at idle.
What's left resident is systemd, udevd, nsncd, networkd, journald, logind, dbus-broker and one getty, about 40MB of userland PSS.
zram with zstd at memoryPercent = 100 capped at 512MB, no disk swap. This, plus the next one, is what makes rebuilding in 512MB possible.
vm.swappiness = 180 so the kernel would rather compress cold anon pages into zram than throw away page cache, vm.page-cluster = 0 since read-ahead on zram is wasted memory, and vm.watermark_scale_factor = 125 with vm.watermark_boost_factor = 0 so kswapd starts earlier and the rebuild doesn't stall in direct reclaim. During a rebuild at 512MB zram peaked at 116MB of real RAM.
Tuned the Boehm GC that Nix uses, set system wide with environment.variables so nixos-rebuild picks it up. Evaluating the module system On a 2GB VM nix-instantiate '<nixpkgs/nixos>' -A system peaked at 599MB stock (Nix 2.34 pre-grows its heap to 25% of RAM, capped at 384MB). GC_INITIAL_HEAP_SIZE=33554432 took it to 597, adding GC_FREE_SPACE_DIVISOR=8 to 562, adding GC_FORCE_UNMAP_ON_GCOLLECT=1 to 548MB. I couldn't find anything else that meaningfully moves eval memory.
Trimmed the closure, which is mostly disk but means less to pull and manage on update: environment.defaultPackages = [ ], documentation off, xdg mime/icons/sounds off, fontconfig off, lvm and bcache off, systemd-importd suppressed (it drags in gnupg, openldap and cyrus-sasl, about 18MB), nixos-option off (man-db and groff, about 11MB), nixos-install/enter/build-vms off, and su.forwardXAuth forced off to lose xauth. Closure went from 963MB to 910MB and the compressed image from 607MB to 477MB.
The one thing 512MB still struggles with is jumping releases (26.05 to unstable). On a 4GB disk the first attempt went on for about 30 minutes before nix-build got OOM-killed, the old generation kept running fine, and running it again finished because everything was already downloaded. If you're doing a release jump give it more RAM for the duration or expect to run it twice and dont bother waiting 30 minutes, just kill it after 5/10 and run it a second time, that said this was to a pre release as thats all I could find to jump too so maybe that had something to do with it.
Full config below. Some of tierhive.nix is platform stuff (cloud-init, password resets, reserved blocks) rather than RAM related, but it's the complete working files.
configuration.nix
{ config, lib, pkgs, ... }:

{
  imports = [
    ./hardware-configuration.nix
    ./tierhive.nix
  ];

  environment.systemPackages = with pkgs; [ curl rsync ];

  system.stateVersion = "26.05";
}
hardware-configuration.nix
{ config, lib, pkgs, modulesPath, ... }:

{
  boot.initrd.includeDefaultModules = false;
  boot.initrd.availableKernelModules = [ "virtio_pci" "virtio_blk" "ext4" ];
  boot.initrd.kernelModules = [ ];
  boot.kernelModules = [ ];
  boot.extraModulePackages = [ ];

  fileSystems."/" = {
    device = "/dev/disk/by-label/nixos";
    fsType = "ext4";
  };

  swapDevices = [ ];

  nixpkgs.hostPlatform = lib.mkDefault "x86_64-linux";
}

title: SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
content:
OCTOBER 29, 2026
SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
The team directly observed a unique property in an altermagnetic candidate material, delivering key evidence of a new phase of magnetism first postulated in 2022.
By Erin Woodward
Subscribe to SLAC Breaking News(external link)
Key takeaways:
The scientific case for a third type of magnetism – termed “altermagnetism” – has been building over recent years. 
Now, a SLAC-led team has experimentally proven that a material exhibits characteristics that are theoretically impossible to explain without altermagnetism. 
Altermagnetic materials could be used to design advanced electronics, with applications including quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers. 
For decades, physicists recognized only two types of magnetism that occur in materials without external influence: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Today, in findings published in Science(external link), a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has delivered conclusive experimental proof of a third magnetic phase called altermagnetism. 
“In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy,” explained lead author Daniel Jost(external link), associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences(external link). “Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase – altermagnetism – is real.” 
Building on previous studies, this research confirmed that manganese telluride (MnTe) is an altermagnet – a new class of magnet that exhibits properties of both ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Their results showed direct experimental evidence of chirality – an asymmetric magnetic structure, akin to a spiral staircase or a screw – in the spins of an altermagnetic candidate material. 
Identifying these unique materials could allow researchers to manipulate their properties in ways that make them ideal candidates for advanced electronics, with applications including quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers. 
A primer on magnetism
To most of us, magnetism is a tangible force: It’s what holds a child's artwork to a refrigerator door and points a compass needle north. But to a physicist, magnetism is more complex. It’s a quantum property of a material, and not all magnetic materials have a directly observable magnetic effect. 
In physics, a material is considered magnetic if its electrons’ spins – their internal angular momentum, which can be either “up” or “down” – are polarized, or ordered in a specific pattern. 
In ferromagnets, all electronic spins point the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down), creating an observable magnetic field. Humans have known about and made use of this class of magnets since ancient times. In 1933, scientists discovered another type of material with polarized spins. Antiferromagnets have alternating electronic spins (up-down-up-down) that cancel each other out, producing no net magnetic effect. 
A new type of magnetism? 
For nearly 90 years, this two-category system dominated our understanding of magnetism. 
But in recent years, researchers have noticed that some materials don’t fit neatly into either category. Certain materials seemed to exhibit features of both antiferromagnetism, such as alternating spin configuration with no net magnetization, and ferromagnetism, such as the ability to use spin currents. These behaviors were once thought to be mutually exclusive. 
In 2022, researchers proposed(external link) the term “altermagnets” to label this wily class of materials.
We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase – altermagnetism – is real. 
Daniel Jost
Associate Scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences
To explain this behavior, researchers postulated that altermagnets exhibit an alternating spin polarization (up-down-up-down), much like conventional antiferromagnets, but with a crucial twist: the crystal lattice structure surrounding the “up” spins is rotated relative to the lattice surrounding the “down” spins. This geometric twist is a break in symmetry that could give rise to their unusual behavior. 
Chirality: the final piece of the puzzle 
“By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real,” Jost said, “but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle.” 
That missing piece was experimental evidence of chirality in an altermagnetic candidate material. Chirality, often referred to as “handedness,” means a material cannot be superimposed on a mirror image of itself, just like a left hand cannot fit into a right-handed glove. 
Chirality offers a clever way to distinguish subtle, quantum-level differences between antiferromagnets and suspected altermagnets: While an altermagnetic material would have alternating spins (up-down-up-down) like an antiferromagnet, the geometric twists in its lattice would give the material’s electronic and magnetic structure a distinct handedness that conventional antiferromagnets lack. 
Jost’s team chose to investigate chirality in MnTe – a material considered antiferromagnetic for decades until a few years ago when it was suspected to be altermagnetic. The team brought it to the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France, to a beamline known for its ability to generate highly controlled polarized X-ray beams. 
“Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams,” explained Jost. “Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way.” 
By scattering circularly polarized X-rays from the material and comparing how it responded to left- versus right-handed light, they teased out a clear chiral signal that shouldn’t exist in a conventional antiferromagnet. 
“This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own,” Jost said. The initial experiment was completed in 2024; the team repeated their experiment in early 2025, confirming their earlier results. 
“This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties,” said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. “Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible.” 
  Rachel Nickel, a postdoctoral fellow at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in France, is part of the team that observed direct evidence of a new class of magnetism called altermagnetism. (ESRF/Stef Candé)
Altermagnetism in the real world 
This discovery has big implications for the field of spintronics, where researchers are leveraging the polarized spin of magnetic materials to design next-generation electronics. 
Where traditional computing technologies use only an electron’s charge to store and move information, spintronics takes advantage of both an electron’s charge and its spin, giving researchers an additional control knob. Spintronic devices have the potential to be faster, be more robust and significantly decrease power consumption in computing and data centers. 
Researchers have had some success with spintronic devices, but that success has been limited by the nature of ferro- and antiferromagnetism. 
“Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields,” Jost explained. “If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible – so you can’t easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents.”
“Altermagnets combine the best of both,” Jost said. “They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with.” 
Future research will explore how altermagnetic states can be influenced and controlled using light and electricity to enhance their usefulness in spintronic solutions for quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.

title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public | TechPolicy.Press
content:
PERSPECTIVE
The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public
MATT SCHERER / NOV 2, 2026
Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Republish
Share
Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings, extensive use of financial engineering, and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.
That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.
The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.
Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.
Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.
The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.
Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense: they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.
Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts, Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.
Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.
Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins
AI industry margins
Demand pressure:
Businesses and consumersmay not be willing to payenough for generative AI.
Commoditization:
Fierce competitionwill make it difficult toraise prices.
Cost pressures:
High costs mean developerscan’t cut prices withouthemorrhaging cash.
External constraints:
Supply-chain challenges andcommunity opposition drive upcosts and delay revenue generation.
Source: Matthew U. Scherer and Maya Jenkins, “Brace for Impact: Protecting People and the Economy When the AI Bubble Bursts,” Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, October 2026 (Figure 13, p. 30).
Interactive graphic: Tech Policy Press
First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies, including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses. Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).
Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid.
Our content delivered to your inbox.
Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy
SUBSCRIBE
Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential.
In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required.
That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion, and the prices for some components are soaring.
That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments.
And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task.
Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher.
Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost.
If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice.
It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite.
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect.” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches.
The SEC should block Anthropic’s stock market debut until the company provides two consecutive quarters of audited financial statements, with all material information about the company’s spending commitments disclosed. Failing to do so could have dire consequences for workers, investors, and ultimately the financial system and economy.

content:

NEWS WHAT'S UP NOV 02, 2026
Tracker. The biggest update yet.
Polyend releases the Tracker firmware source code
Today we’re publishing the firmware source code for the original Tracker, Tracker+ and Tracker Mini on GitHub. We’re also releasing Tracker Community Edition 1.0 with tons of new features and improvements. You can install it on any of the three instruments, modify the firmware yourself and share your own version. We’ve built in a recovery system to keep a faulty firmware build from bricking your Tracker.
Explore the Tracker Community Edition repository on GitHub
Here at Polyend, creativity is what we value most. We’ve seen it firsthand in the unofficial Tracker mods you’ve built, and we’re sharing the firmware source code to support that work. Maybe you want to build an entirely new instrument on the Tracker hardware. Or maybe there’s just one thing you wish your Tracker did differently. Either way, you can now try it on the unit you already own. I bet some of you already have ideas for the original Tracker that never crossed our minds.
Piotr Raczyński, CEO of Polyend
Click to accept marketing cookies and enable this content
What’s new in Community Edition 1.0
Stream long samples from the SD card. Bring full-length stems, loops and field recordings into a project using a fraction of the sample memory they’d normally need. This works even on the original Tracker.
Record timing and velocity while keeping both step FX slots free. Micro-move and Volume now have dedicated fields on every step. New Chance conditions let you bring in a snare fill every fourth pass.
Load plugins in the Sample Editor. Six effects and generators are included, from an analog-style kick generator to a stereo delay. The plugin SDK lets you build, share and sell your own.
Play two new synths on Tracker+ and Tracker Mini. CHIP and DIRT join the synth lineup. A new SDK lets you build your own synth engines.
All three models also get wavetable envelopes and LFOs, faster project loading and saving, and tighter MIDI clock timing. You can design custom Tracker themes and fonts in your browser.

title: Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432 · freenode
content:
SELF-HOSTED
By relay
OCTOBER 31, 2026
Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432
No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating.
L
Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432, a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update.
Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables.
Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.
